ApiVersion.description: Contract schema version. Only `v1` exists today.

ColType.description: Column data type as declared in the contract.

ColumnDef.description: Definition of a single column in the contract.

classification.description: Data classification (reserved, FR-11 — no engine behavior in v1).

description.description:
What the column means, in a sentence the supplier would recognise.

The engine never reads this. It exists because the expensive half of a broken delivery is the argument about what the column was supposed to contain, and that argument is settled by a sentence written before anything broke. ODCS carries the same field on a property, so it survives a round trip in both directions.

pii.description: PII tag (reserved, FR-11 — no engine behavior in v1).

required.description: If `true`, the column must not contain nulls.

stability.description:
How much a consumer may rely on this column staying as it is.

Absent means [`Stability::Stable`] — the promise every column has always carried, stated out loud rather than assumed.

sunset.description:
The date after which this column will no longer be here, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

Held as a string rather than a date type on purpose: this crate parses contracts on machines that may have no clock worth trusting, and it has no business deciding what "today" is. [`crate::validate`](fn@crate::validate) proves the shape and the calendar; ISO-8601 sorts lexicographically, which is all the diff needs to tell a date that moved closer from one that moved away. Anything that acts on the date — refusing a change, chasing the consumers who still read the column — does it where a clock exists.

Consumer.description:
A downstream consumer of the dataset.

The validation engine still never reads this — a consumer changes no verdict. What [`Consumer::reads`] adds is the other half of the sentence a contract is for: not only what the supplier promised, but who inside your own company is standing behind that promise. It is what lets a tool answer *who breaks* when a column is dropped or a delivery fails on it.

contact.description: Contact for the consumer (email, Slack channel, …).

kind.description:
What this consumer is — see [`ConsumerKind`].

Absent stays absent. There is no sensible default here: guessing `pipeline` for a consumer whose author said nothing would print a category somebody could act on and nobody wrote down.

reads.description:
The columns this consumer depends on.

**Empty means the whole dataset**, and that is the honest default: a consumer who has not said which columns they read is a consumer who might break on any of them, and quietly narrowing their blast radius to nothing would make an unanswered question look like a safe answer. Say the columns and the answer gets sharper — a change to `region` stops paging the team that only reads `amount`.

Every name must be a column the contract declares; [`crate::validate`](fn@crate::validate) rejects the rest, because a typo here is a dependency that silently matches nothing, which is worse than no declaration at all.

tier.description:
How much depends on this one, from 1 (most) to 3 (least).

Deliberately three numbers and not a free-text severity. The point of a tier is to be *comparable* across two consumers nobody has ever had to compare before — the moment somebody has to choose which of two teams finds out first. A scale with five levels, or with words, is a scale where everything ends up in the top two.

Absent means it has not been ranked, which is not the same as tier 3. [`crate::validate`](fn@crate::validate) proves the range; nothing here decides what a tier is worth, because that is a decision each organisation makes.

ConsumerKind.description:
What a consumer *is*.

"Three consumers" is a number. "A tier-1 dashboard, a model and an internal report" is a decision, and it is a different decision in each case: a dashboard that goes blank is embarrassing on a Monday morning, a model that silently retrains on a changed column is wrong for a quarter, and an agent reading the dataset over an API has nobody watching it at all.

The engine never reads this — a kind changes no verdict. It changes what the sentence says when somebody has to decide whether to approve a tightening today or wait until the window closes.

oneOf.description: A chart somebody looks at. Breaks visibly, and to an audience.
A trained or scheduled model. Breaks quietly, and keeps running.
A service serving this data onward. Its own consumers are not in here.
A scheduled job. Usually fails loudly, at 3am.
An autonomous workload reading this without a person in the loop.
A document produced on a schedule. Wrong quietly, and circulated.

DataClass.description:
Data classification level of a column.

Reserved field (PRD FR-11) — no engine behavior in v1.

EnumValue.description: A scalar value allowed inside an `enum` check.

FixedWidthField.description:
One field of a fixed-width record: a name and the character positions (1-based, inclusive) it occupies on every line.

Give `end` or `width`, not both. `start` may be left out on every field but the first, in which case the field begins right after the previous one — the way a layout document usually reads.

name.description: Column name the field is read into.

start.description: First character position, 1-based. Defaults to the character after the previous field's end (1 for the first field).

width.description: Number of characters, as an alternative to `end`.

InputFormat.description: The on-disk format of a dataset's feed, when the contract pins it (`settings.input.format`). Without it the reader goes by the file extension, which is right for almost everything except a feed that arrives as `export.dat`.

oneOf.description: An Excel workbook (`.xlsx`, `.xlsm`, `.xlsb`, `.xls`) or OpenDocument spreadsheet (`.ods`). One sheet is the dataset; see `sheet`.
An XML document with one element per record; see `xml_record`.
Fixed-width text, one record per line, columns by character position; see `fixed_width`.

InputSettings.description:
How the feed is read (`settings.input`). Everything here is optional and most contracts need none of it: a `.csv` is a CSV. It exists for the feeds that need telling — the workbook whose data is on the third sheet under two title rows, the XML export whose records are `<Order>` elements, the mainframe extract with no delimiters at all.

Reading instructions belong in the contract rather than on the command line because the contract is what travels: the same file read the same way in CI, in the cloud's SFTP pickup and on a laptop, without each remembering the flags.

delimiter.description: CSV/TSV: the field delimiter, one character (default `,` for CSV, tab for TSV). Write a tab as `"\t"`.

fixed_width.description: Fixed-width: the fields, in the order they lie on the line.

format.description: Pin the format instead of going by the file extension.

has_header.description: CSV/TSV/Excel/fixed-width: whether the first row names the columns. Default `true`, except fixed-width, where the fields carry the names and the default is `false`.

json_path.description: JSON: dotted path to the record array inside a wrapping object (`data.items`).

sheet.description: Excel: the sheet holding the data, by name or 1-based position (default: the first sheet).

skip_rows.description: Excel/CSV/fixed-width: rows to skip before the header (title rows, blank lines a report writer leaves at the top).

xml_record.description: XML: the element that is one record — a name (`order`) or a path from the root (`orders/order`). Default: the root's first child element.

KnownFormat.description: Built-in value formats accepted by the `format` check.

anyOf.description: Inclusive min/max bounds; either side may be omitted.

LengthSpec.description: String-length constraint: exact (`length: 2`) or a range (`length: { min: 1, max: 10 }`).

Migration.description:
The window a supplier gives consumers to get ready for a breaking change.

A breaking change with a date attached is a plan. The same change without one is an outage that has not happened yet, and the difference between them is not the diff — it is whether anybody downstream was told when.

This block is about *this version*: what it broke, and by when everyone reading it has to have moved. It is expected to be dropped again once the window closes, so a later version losing it is not itself an event.

note.description: What consumers have to actually do, in their words rather than the diff's. "`amount` is minor units from 15 Oct; read `amount_minor` today" is the sentence that saves the calls.

window_ends.description:
The date consumers must be ready by, as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

Required, and deliberately so. A migration block without a deadline is a promise to deal with it later, which is the thing it exists to replace.

Number.description: A YAML number: integer or float. `min: 18` parses as [`Number::Int`], `min: 18.5` as [`Number::Float`], and each serializes back the same way.

PiiKind.description:
Kind of personally identifiable information stored in a column.

Reserved field (PRD FR-11): parsed, validated, and echoed into results — no engine behavior until Phase 2 (blast radius, compliance evidence).

oneOf.description: PII not covered by the other kinds.

allow_extra_columns.description: Whether columns not declared in the contract are allowed (default `true`).

columns_exact.description: Whether the dataset must contain *exactly* the declared columns (default `false`).

input.description: How the feed is read — format, sheet, XML record element, fixed-width layout. Left out of YAML output when nothing is set.

on_type_mismatch.description: Severity applied when a value cannot be read as the declared type (default `error`).

Severity.description: Severity of a failed check: `error` fails the run, `warn` is reported only.

oneOf.description: The check failing makes the run fail (exit code 1). Default.
The check failing is reported but does not fail the run (unless `--strict`).

Stability.description:
How much a consumer is entitled to rely on a column.

The contract already says what a column *is*. This says how long it can be counted on to stay that way, which is the question a consumer has to answer before building anything on it — and which, until now, they could only answer by asking somebody.

It also gives a supplier the one move they did not have: retiring a column on purpose. Removing a column has always been a breaking change and always will be. Announcing months ahead that it is going, with a date, turns that breaking change from something that happens *to* consumers into something they were given time to prepare for.

oneOf.description: The default, and what every column without the field means. It will not be removed or retyped without the notice a breaking change gets.
Offered, not promised. Read it if you like; it may move without the ceremony a stable column gets.
On its way out. `sunset` says when.

description: A parsed data contract (the root of `contract.yaml`).

consumers.description: Downstream consumers (reserved, FR-11 — no engine behavior in v1).

dataset.description: Dataset name; part of the contract's identity.

migration.description:
The migration window for the breaking changes this version introduces.

Optional, because most versions break nothing. A project can require it for the ones that do — see the cloud's review settings.

primary_key.description:
The column (or columns, in order) that identify one row.

Declaring it does two things: every delivery is checked for the key being present on every row and never repeated (`dataset.primary_key`), and other contracts can point at this one with `references`.
